content.overview: Mens rea is the guilty mind. Most BNS offences specify intention, knowledge, dishonesty, fraud, rashness or negligence. The statute’s verb is the answer — not the Latin label.
content.glance: Mens rea is the guilty mind. Most BNS offences specify intention, knowledge, dishonesty, fraud, rashness or negligence. The statute’s verb is the answer — not the Latin label.
content.study:
Topic at a glance
[[REF:DOCTRINE:CRIMINAL-LAW:MENS-REA]] is a family name. Indian criminal law is statutory: read the section.

Why it exists
A civil wrong can be committed by accident. A crime, as a rule, should not. The BNS therefore writes a fault element into almost every offence, and then lists the cases (Chapter III) where the mind is missing or excused.

How to read a section
1. Find the verb: “intentionally”, “knowingly”, “voluntarily”, “dishonestly”, “fraudulently”, “rashly”, “negligently”.
2. That verb is the mens rea you must prove.
3. [[REF:DOCTRINE:CRIMINAL-LAW:COMMON-INTENTION]] shares that mind among several persons; it does not replace it.
4. Strict liability exists only where the text is clear — typically public-welfare / regulatory offences, not homicide.

Capacity
[[REF:CONCEPT:CRIMINAL-LAW:DOLI-INCAPAX]]: under 7, s. 20 is conclusive. 7–12, s. 21 needs maturity of understanding. Unsoundness of mind is s. 22 (McNaghten core). Intoxication is s. 23–24: involuntary intoxication can excuse; voluntary drunkenness does not, except on the specific intent enquiry.

Current-law position
The BNS did not abolish mens rea. It restated it in Indian English. Do not write that “the new Code is strict liability”.

Educational note
Name the section’s word in the exam. “Mens rea” alone scores half.

provisions.title: Act of a child under seven years of age

examples.title: Example 1 — simple
examples.body: A takes B’s umbrella in a restaurant, honestly believing it is his. There is no “dishonestly” for theft (s. 303). The taking without that mind is not theft.

examples.title: Example 2 — legal
examples.body: A drives at high speed through a market and kills a pedestrian. If the prosecution proves only rashness, s. 106. If it proves knowledge that death was likely, the case climbs toward s. 100/105.

hypotheticals.question: Does A commit an offence?
hypotheticals.analysis: s. 20 does not apply (A is not under 7). s. 21 requires that the child has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge the nature and consequences of conduct. Literacy is not the test. If the Court finds A did not understand that throwing at a train could injure, there is no offence. If it finds he did, the mental element of the charged section must still be proved.

rows.left: Did the accused want the consequence, or know it was likely?
rows.right: Did the accused take a risk a prudent person would not?

misconceptions.trap: Every BNS offence is strict liability.
misconceptions.correction: Most offences have a stated mental element. Strict liability is the exception.
Quote the section: dishonestly, intentionally, knowingly, rashly.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What is the first step in proving mens rea under the BNS?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Read the verb in the section and prove that mental element. The Latin label is not a substitute.

cases.name: State of Maharashtra v. Mayer Hans George
cases.holding: Statutory offences may exclude mens rea where the statute is clear — typically public-welfare / foreign-exchange type offences. Do not generalise this to the BNS homicide scheme.
cases.relevance: The exception that proves the rule. Use only when the section is silent and regulatory.

cases.name: Mahbub Shah v. Emperor
cases.holding: Common intention is a sharing of mens rea, not a substitute for it.

learningObjectives: Identify the mental element expressly required by a criminal provision.
Distinguish intention, knowledge, dishonesty, fraud, rashness and negligence by reading the offence text.
Explain why mens rea is a statutory question in Indian criminal law.
Use the doctrine to structure a problem answer rather than treating the Latin label as the conclusion.
enhancement.definition: Mens rea refers to the mental element required by the offence. In Indian statutory criminal law, the precise requirement must be derived from the wording and structure of the applicable provision rather than assumed from the label alone.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The student should identify the exact mental element demanded by the offence, then prove it from the facts and evidence. General propositions about mens rea do not displace a statutory requirement.
statutoryFramework: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — s. 2 definitions and s. 3 general explanations, as applicable to the offence.
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — Chapter III general exceptions, including the statutory rules concerning capacity and mental condition.
Always read the particular offence provision to determine its operative mental element.
essentialIngredients: Separate the mental element from the physical act or consequence.
Test the evidence against the required state of mind.
Check any express statutory exception or qualification.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Mens rea is most useful as an analytical method. The examiner should see the statutory word, its legal meaning, the fact that proves it, and the conclusion that follows. For example, if an offence requires knowledge, the answer should ask what the accused knew and what evidence establishes that knowledge. If it requires dishonesty, the answer should apply the statutory definition rather than substitute a general idea of bad faith. The same method prevents a common mistake: treating every offence as if it required the same mental state.
examples: If the provision requires knowledge, identify the surrounding facts from which knowledge may be inferred.
If the provision requires dishonesty, apply the statutory definition and explain whose property/economic interest is affected and what the accused intended.
If the provision expressly creates an offence based on rash or negligent conduct, analyse that wording rather than importing an intention standard.
distinctions: Intention vs. knowledge: intention focuses on the desired consequence or conduct; knowledge concerns awareness of the relevant fact or likely consequence, subject to the wording of the provision.
Mens rea vs. motive: motive may explain why a person acted but is not automatically the mental element required by the offence.
Mens rea vs. actus reus: the physical conduct/consequence and the required mental state are separate analytical components.
caseLaw: State of Maharashtra v. Mayer Hans George, AIR 1965 SC 722 — Supreme Court authority commonly cited on statutory offences and the question whether mens rea is excluded by the statutory scheme; use it cautiously and in context.
Mahbub Shah v. Emperor, AIR 1945 PC 118 — historical authority on common intention; useful for distinguishing shared intention from the mental element of the substantive offence.
problemApplication: Underline or identify the operative mental-state word.
State its legal meaning from the statute.

Address the strongest alternative explanation for the accused's state of mind.
Conclude only after separately analysing the act and the mental element.

shortAnswer: State that the exact mental element comes from the offence provision.

keyTakeaways: The statutory verb matters more than the Latin label.
Always separate actus reus from the required mental element.
Do not confuse motive with mens rea.
